analysis.one_liner: Caps compensation for patients injured by medical negligence, capping pain-and-suffering awards at $250,000.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2001 with 5 Republican cosponsors, the bill never received a committee hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set national rules for medical malpractice lawsuits, overriding state laws: pain-and-suffering awards would be capped at $250,000, punitive damages would require near-criminal proof of intent and be capped, payments the patient already received from insurance would be subtracted from any award, and lawyers could charge no more than 25% of a recovery. The stated goal was to lower malpractice insurance premiums and keep health care affordable, but the practical effect would be to reduce what injured patients can recover and make malpractice lawsuits harder and less profitable to bring.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers. Malpractice insurers would pay out less in claims; providers would face lower premiums and less exposure to large jury verdicts; plaintiffs' attorneys could no longer charge above 25% of a recovery.

how_it_helps.text: Caps non-economic damages (pain, suffering, disfigurement, loss of companionship) at $250,000 total regardless of how severe the injury or how many defendants are involved.

Allows punitive damages only when proven by clear and convincing evidence of intent to injure, deliberate failure to avoid certain injury, or conscious disregard of a substantial risk — a far higher bar than ordinary negligence — and caps them at the greater of 3 times economic damages or $250,000.

Requires any payment from health insurance or other sources to be subtracted from a malpractice award, and makes each defendant liable only for their own percentage of fault rather than jointly liable for the full award.
Caps attorneys' fees at 25% of any judgment or settlement, and would override any state law that is less restrictive, subject to a process allowing states to opt out for in-state cases.
The bill's stated purpose is to ensure fair compensation for meritorious claims, improve availability of health care where liability suits have reduced it, and reduce unpredictable compensation.

analysis.who_pays: Patients seriously injured by medical negligence. A child with lifelong brain damage from a delivery error would be limited to $250,000 for pain and suffering plus economic losses; insurance payments would be subtracted from the recovery; and a lower fee cap could make it harder to find a lawyer willing to take a complex case.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on non-economic damages applies no matter how severe the harm — disfigurement, chronic pain, or loss of a child — and states could not set higher protections for cases they chose to keep under the federal rules, so the bill preempts state tort law in many situations.

Mandatory subtraction of collateral source payments means a patient whose health insurer already covered medical bills recovers less than the actual harm caused, effectively shifting costs to the patient's own insurance.
Making liability several-only means if one negligent defendant is insolvent or a doctor's share cannot be collected, the injured patient absorbs the shortfall.
The bill would apply even to injuries that occurred before its enactment, covering any case filed after the law took effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Lower malpractice premiums and less defensive medicine were the stated goals, and damage caps have historically reduced insurer payouts. But the bill achieved that by shifting the cost onto the most severely injured patients, who lose the largest share of their compensation, and it did so with a national preemption of state tort law. Whatever premium savings resulted, the design places the burden on the people with the most serious claims.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2001, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Mitch McConnell introduced the bill on August 3, 2001; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
Five Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
The Judiciary Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Malpractice insurers and health care providers kept paying under the existing system, but injured patients were the more direct beneficiaries of the bill's failure: they kept whatever state-law rights to full compensation their states allowed. Plaintiffs' attorneys also avoided the 25% fee cap that would have reduced their contingency income.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred, chaired by Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-VT)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — leaving the bill without a path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrats signed on, but no roll-call vote was ever taken, so the full Senate never revealed where it stood.

industries.note: Damage caps, punitive-damages limits, and mandatory offsets would directly reduce the claims insurers must pay, while the premiums charged to doctors and hospitals are the insurers' revenue. Insurers gain by paying injured patients less.

industries.industry: Physicians, hospitals, and other health care providers
industries.note: Providers would face lower liability exposure and, they argued, lower malpractice premiums. Their gain comes directly out of what injured patients can recover, though the bill framed the trade as better health care access.

The 25% fee cap, the higher proof standard for punitive damages, and the compensation caps shrink the size and number of contingency cases, reducing attorneys' income. Attorneys' financial interest here runs alongside their injured clients'.

Mandatory collateral source offsets mean payments health insurers already made for a patient's care are deducted from malpractice awards, so patients recover less from the negligent party and their insurer's costs stay where they are.
